case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12-3-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1915 of 2000.).
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana, J: This Civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 12-3-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1915 of 2000 making the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and decree dated 3-2-2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 489 of 1999 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 18-7-1999 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 190 of 1998 dismissing the suit.

2. Md Ibrahim (the predecessor-in-interest of the present appellant), as plaintiff, instituted the above mentioned Title Suit No. 190 of 1998 impleading the respondent herein as the sole defendant for declaration that the defendant is 'benamder' of the plaintiff in respect of the properties described in schedule `Ka' and 'Kha' to the plaint and also for declaration of his title in those properties. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land of schedule 'Ka' originally belonged to Samon Rishi and CS Khatian was prepared in his name. Samon Rishi died leaving two sons, named Hari Mohan and Rai Mohan. Hari Mohan died leaving wife Brahmo Rishi and son Bhagoban Rishi. Bhagoban Rishi died unmarried leaving mother Brohma Rishi as sole heir. That Brahmo Rishi while in possession of her share sold out that to Adu Bepari by kabala dated 14-5-1920. That Rai Mohan, the other son of Samon Rishi died leaving five sons, namely, Rajendra, Kutishar, Naba Rishi, Debendra and Surja Mohan and wife Bidhya Rishi. The said heirs of Rai Mohan transferred their share in favour of Adu Bepari by three registered sale deeds dated 16-7-1920, 18-8-1920 and 12-1-1921. That Adu Bepari thus became the owner of those lands. Adu Bepari leased out 0.0636 acre of land to Nobendra Rishi, Broja Kumar Rishi and Shita Nath Rishi and kept the remaining 0.0774 acre of land in his khas possession. Subsequently Adu Bepari sold out those 0.0774 acre of land to Ganga Charan Saha by kabala dated 12-6-1923. Ganga Charan Saha subsequently sold that land to Bhagaban Chandra Bhowmik by kabala dated 26-1-1927. Bhagaban Chandra Bhowmik subsequently transferred the said land to Kanai Lal Gope by kabala dated 22-2-1939. Kanai Lal Gope while in possession, leased out the same land to the plaintiff by registered deed of lease dated 11-4-1952; said Kanai Lal Gope executed a deed of sale also in respect of the said property in favour of the plaintiff on 12-4-1952 which was registered on the same date. That the plaintiff, out of love and affection, purchased the said land in the name of the defendant who is his cousin and sister-in-law; that plaintiff paid the entire consideration money and purchased the same for his own interest and benefit; that the defendant had no means to pay the consideration. That to maintain the benami character of the suit land the plaintiff had the subsequent record of rights recorded in the name of his 'benamdar'. The plaintiff is in possession of the 'Ka' schedule land. He established a mill under the name and style "Ibrahim Machinery Manufacturing Company" in this 'Ka' scheduled land.

3. Plaintiffs further case is that the 'Kha' scheduled land belonged to Upendra Chandra Rishi who transferred the said land to the plaintiff by registered sale deed dated 14-1-1964 and also delivered possession of the said land to the plaintiff. That subsequently the successors of said Upendra Chandra Rishi again executed and registered a deed of sale dated 28-8-1970 in favour of the plaintiff. That the plaintiff purchased this land also for his own benefit out of his own fund, but took the kabala in the 'benami' of the defendant. That the original kabala was in the custody of the plaintiff, but recently when the survey operation was going on the plaintiff carried the kabala to show the same to the survey officials and on way back the same was lost. That the original lease deed as well as the sale deed in respect of 'Ka' scheduled land also were in custody of the plaintiff; the plaintiff, for the purpose of obtaining loan against the said land, applied to the House Building Finance Corporation and along with the application for loan the original lease deed also was submitted, but the loan application was rejected; as the document was in the name of the defendant the plaintiff took it back from the House Building Finance Corporation through her; that the defendant although promised to return that document later on, but subsequently, being ill advised, refused to return the same and claimed title in the suit land. That the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property by running a mill on part of the suit land and by letting out houses thereon to different tenants. That the defendant has no manner of right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, but as she claimed the suit property, the plaintiff has been constrained to file the suit.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the defendant was married to a rich family of Joinpur, India but her husband died after few years of their marriage and the defendant inherited property from her husband; thereafter she, along with her parents and sister (wife of the plaintiff) came to Calcutta and subsequently, after partition of India in 1947, they came to Dhaka; that her brother Hazi Md Siddique came along with them who purchased two separate houses for his sisters out of their money and the defendant purchased the suit land through her brother; that subsequently the plaintiff came and wanted to stay with them who was allowed to stay and was entrusted to look after the property, but the plaintiff fraudulently got the trade license in his name; that the defendant's brother Hazi Md Siddique imported machineries from Delhi to set up the factory, but the plaintiff sold out those machineries and got a plan approved from RAJUK for construction of a multi-storied building on the suit land for which he took Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) from the defendant; that the plaintiff, with a view to grab the suit property, has filed the suit on false and concocted allegations and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. Both the parties adduced some evidence, both oral and documentary to prove their respective case. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellate court below decreed the suit finding the plaintiffs case proved. In revision, the High Court Division set-aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below and restored those of the trial court.

6. Leave to appeal against this judgment of the High Court Division was granted by this Division to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-leave-petitioner mainly to the effect that the appellate court below, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties and also the very fact that the defendant did not deny the plaintiffs case that he purchased the 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant, rightly decreed the suit, but the High Court Division without referring any evidence on record and pointing out any non-consideration or mis-appreciation of evidence on record by the court of appeal below erroneously and illegally set-aside the well-reasoned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below.

7. Mr Anwarul Azim Khair, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant has made submissions before us to the effect that in this suit for declaration of a transaction as 'benami' the plaintiff adduced sufficient evidence-both oral and documentary-to prove all the factors necessary for proving benami purchases; that the evidence adduced by the plaintiff have proved clearly that he paid the consideration money and he has also been possessing the suit land since his purchase; that the plaintiff has also produced the kabala deed showing purchase of the suit land and all other previous transfer deeds relating to the suit land. The learned Advocate has argued that the appellate court below, the last court of facts, on consideration of all these evidence adduced by the plaintiff and also the evidence adduced by the defendant and other facts and circumstances decreed the suit on making elaborate discussion of evidence and also assigning reasons, but the High Court Division without adverting to the reasonings arrived at by the appellate court below and also without considering the evidence adduced by the parties at all most whimsically set-aside the well-reasoned judgment of the appellate court below and restored those of the trial court. The learned Advocate has argued that the judgment of the trial court, in fact, is no judgment at all in the eye of law inasmuch as in this judgment the huge evidence adduced by the plaintiff was not considered at all, that the trial court dismissed the suit on the main reasoning that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant and that the title deed of the suit land came from the custody of the defendant and that the plaintiffs wife deposed in this suit supporting the case of the defendant. The learned Advocate has argued also that the High Court Division committed more wrong and illegality in restoring the judgment and decree of the trial court making observations to the effect that the plaintiff did not examine a single witness to prove his alleged 'benami' purchase of the suit land and to prove the payment of consideration money by him. The learned Advocate has argued that these observations of the High Court Division are absolutely wrong inasmuch as in this suit the plaintiff examined as many as six-witnesses and also adduced bundle of documentary evidence which have been marked as exhibit and all of which have proved sufficiently that the plaintiff purchased the suit land and he paid the consideration money; that the High Court Division also without examining the evidence on record most illegally and erroneously held that the title deed of the suit land came from the custody of the defendant. The learned Advocate has made submissions to the effect also that in this suit the plaintiffs specific case is that Kanai Lal Gope-the original owner of the suit land settled the suit land with him by a registered lease deed dated 11-4-1952 and on the same date he also sold his rent receiving interest in the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by registered kabala and that the plaintiff took that kabala also in the name of the defendant, but the defendant could produce the lease deed only in respect of the suit land which has been marked as Exhibit-'Ka' and the kabala deed-the exahibit-13 and all other previous transfer deeds in respect of the suit land and also the rent receipts, tax receipts, electricity bills, gas bills, water bills etc. in respect of the suit land came before court from the custody of this plaintiff, but neither the trial court nor the High Court Division took into consideration this most important fact that a bundle of title deeds and also various receipts in respect of the suit land came from the custody of the plaintiff, rather the High Court Division, in the impugned judgment most erroneously held that the plaintiff could not adduce any document or any other proof to prove his purchase of the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has made submissions to the effect also that in this suit the admitted facts are that the defendant is the cousin and also the sister-in-law of the plaintiff and that the plaintiff being issueless was very much affectionate to the defendant who lost her husband at her tender age and thereafter used to reside with the plaintiff and his wife in the same house. The learned Advocate has made argument to the effect also that in this suit the plaintiff claimed to have purchased both the 'Ka' scheduled land and 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant and the defendant though denied the claim of the plaintiff in respect of the `Ka' scheduled land only, but she did not raise any claim in respect of the `Kha' scheduled land and thereby she rather admitted the plaintiff's case that he purchased the 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant. The learned Advocate has argued that this very admitted fact that the plaintiff purchased the `Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant was ignored by both the trial court and the High Court Division though this fact was very much important in this suit to be considered. The learned Advocate has contended that this very admitted fact that the plaintiff purchased the 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant coupled with the evidence adduced by the plaintiff prove sufficiently that the plaintiff purchased the 'Ka' scheduled land also in the 'benami' of the defendant. The learned Advocate has argued that the appellate court below, on consideration of all these facts and circumstances and evidence on record rightly decreed the suit of the plaintiff, but the High Court Division without at all adverting to these findings and decision of the appellate court below and also the reasonings thereof most arbitrarily and illegally set-aside the well-reasoned judgment of the appellate court below and restored that of the trial court which was not at all sustainable in law.

8. Mr Md Asaduzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-respondent has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. The learned Advocate has made argument to the effect that both the trial court and the High Court Division rightly disbelieved the plaintiffs case of his 'benami' purchase of the 'Ka' scheduled property. The learned Advocate has argued that in fact there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant who was his sister-in-law; that the own wife of the plaintiff has deposed in this suit as DW 2 denying the claim of the plaintiff and stating that the defendant purchased the 'Ka' scheduled land with her own money; that both the trial court and the High Court Division, on consideration of evidence of the plaintiff's wife and other facts and circumstances rightly disbelieved the case of the plaintiff and rightly dismissed the suit; that the appellate court below on misinterpretation and mis-appreciation of the evidence on record decreed the suit of the plaintiff illegally. The learned Advocate has made argument to the effect that the impugned judgment of the High Court Division concurring with the findings and decision of the trial court does not suffer from any wrong or infirmity and, as such, this appeal is liable to dismissed.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, those of the appellate court below and the trial court and the evidence on record.

10. It appears that in this suit the plaintiff has examined as many as six-witnesses and also produced bundle of documents in order to prove his case. On the other hand, the defendant examined three-witnesses only including herself, her sister (the wife of the plaintiff) and her brother's son and a single document the Exhibit-`Ka', the lease deed in respect of the suit land. However, it appears that neither the trial court nor the High Court Division has made any discussion at all about the huge evidence adduced by the plaintiff. The trial court dismissed the suit on the reasonings that (i) there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant, (ii) that the lease deed-the Exhibit-'Ka' in respect of the suit land came from the custody of the defendant and (iii) that the plaintiff's wife deposed against the plaintiff. The High Court Division also appears to have concurred with these reasonings of the trial court and made further observation to the effect that the plaintiff did not examine a single witness to prove his alleged 'benami' purchase of the suit land and also to prove that he paid tote consideration money. The High Court Division made observation to the effect also that the plaintiff could not adduce any document or any other proof to prove his alleged 'benami' purchase of the suit land.

11. Obviously, both the trial court and the High Court Division committed great wrong, illegality and injustice also to make such observations and findings without taking into consideration at all the huge evidence adduced by the plaintiff. Both the trial court and the High Court Division disbelieved the plaintiffs case of 'benami' purchase of the suit land on the main reasoning that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant-his sister-in-law. Both the trial court and the High Court Division did not take into consideration at all that in this suit it is rather an admitted fact that the plaintiff purchased the 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant. Where the defendant did not deny the fact that the plaintiff purchased the `Kha' scheduled land in her 'benami' the trail court and the High Court Division should not have disbelieved the plaintiffs 'benami' purchase of 'Ka' scheduled land on the reasoning that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant. In this suit the undisputed facts are that the defendant is the cousin and also sister-in-law of the plaintiff and the plaintiff, being issueless, was affectionate to the defendant who lost her husband at her tender age and used to live with the plaintiff and his wife in the same house. It is also in evidence that the plaintiff purchased some property in the 'benami' of his wife also. The trial court and the High Court Division did not take into consideration all these facts and consequently disbelieved the plaintiffs case of 'benami' purchase of the 'Ka' scheduled land on the reasoning that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase this land in the 'benami' of the defendant.

12. In a suit for declaration of a 'benami' purchase the main questions which need determination are (i) who paid the consideration money, (ii) from whose custody the title deed comes before court and who is in possession of the property in question. It appears that in this suit the plaintiff has adduced sufficient evidence, both oral and documentary, to have the answers of all these three questions in his favour.

13. Plaintiffs case is that Kanai Lal Gope transferred the suit land by two registered deeds dated 12-4-1952, of which one is lease deed and another is kabala deed, in favour of the plaintiff. The defendant has produced the lease deed only before the court which has been marked as Exhibit-'Ka'; On the other hand the plaintiff has produced the kabala deed dated 12-5-1952 in respect of the suit land which has been marked as Exhibit-13. The plaintiff has also filed the title deed of the vendor Kanai Lal Gope and also the title deeds of the predecessors-in-interest of Kanai Lal Cope in respect of the suit land which all have been marked as Exhibits-2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The defendant could not give any explanation even why all those previous title deeds in respect of the suit land in the names of the previous owners of the suit land came before court from the custody of the plaintiff and why those title deeds in respect of the suit land were not in her custody. Admittedly, the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and he has a factory there in his own name and has been running business therefrom. Though the defendant claimed that she established that factory and business in the suit land through her brother, but no iota of evidence the defendant could produce before court to prove her such case. The plaintiff has produced also bundle of water bills, gas bills, electricity bills and also tax receipts, rent receipts etc. in respect of the suit land which all have been marked as Exhibits-10, 11 and 12 series in this suit. The defendant could not adduce any evidence to prove that she ever paid the holding tax, rent and other bills for the suit land. Save and except the Exhibit-'Ka' only-the lease deed in respect of the suit land-the defendant could not produce any documentary evidence at all in support of her claim in the suit land. The plaintiff has given an explanation as to coming of the lease deed-the Exhibit-'Ka' from the custody of the defendant. He has categorically stated both in the plaint and in the deposition to the effect that he applied for loan to the House Building Finance Corporation and with that loan application he filed that lease deed also and subsequently when his application for loan was rejected he asked the defendant to take back that lease deed from House Building Finance Corporation since that lease deed stood in the name of the defendant and the defendant accordingly took back that lease, deed from the House Building Finance Corporation, but did not hand over that to the plaintiff telling that she would give back that lease deed later, but subsequently, at the ill advice of some other persons, she denied to give back that lease deed to the plaintiff.

14. However, apart from the above mentioned bundle of documentary evidence the plaintiff examined six-witnesses also, all of whom deposed before the court supporting the plaintiffs case.

15. The PW 1 is the plaintiff, Md Ibrahim himself. He has deposed before court in support of his case.

16. The PW 2 has deposed to the effect that the plaintiff possesses the suit land. This witness has deposed further to the effect that on 2-1-1998 the plaintiff demanded the title deed from the defendant, but the defendant refused to give that. During cross-examination this witness has stated further to the effect that the defendant having talked with her brother's son denied to give that title deed to the plaintiff.

17. The PW 3 has deposed to the effect that the suit land is in possession of the plaintiff and that all of that locality know that the suit land belongs to the plaintiff. This witness deposed also that the tenants of the plaintiff are in possession of the suit land. During cross-examination this witness has denied the defence suggestion that the defendant is in possession of the suit land.

18. The PW 4 has deposed to the effect that he is a tenant of the suit land under the plaintiff and that the other tenants also of the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land. To this plaintiffs witness a suggestion was put to the effect that the plaintiff though is in possession of the suit land, but he is not the owner of the same. This witness has denied this defence suggestion.

19. The PW 5 has deposed to the effect that he knew Kanai Lal Gope and that Kanai Lal Gope settled the suit land with the plaintiff and also executed a kabala transferring rent receiving interest to the plaintiff; that on 11-4-1952 the plaintiff gave the lease money and consideration money of kabala to Kanai Lal Gope in his presence; that on 12-4-1952 those deeds were registered and Kanai Lal Gope handed over possession of the suit land to the plaintiff Md Ibrahim on that date. That the plaintiff showed his sister-in-law as the recipients in those deeds; that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since then. This witness has been cross-examined on behalf of the defendant, but by cross-examining this witness nothing could be extracted from him to make him unreliable.

20. The PW 6 has deposed in support of the claim of the plaintiff in respect of the 'Kha' scheduled land which the defendant did not deny.

21. On the other hand, the defendant has examined 3 witnesses only. The DW 1, is the defendant Asma Khatun. This witness has aeposed in support of her case. In course of cross-examination this witness has stated that there is a factory in the suit land since its purchase and that the plaintiff realizes rents from the tenants. Of course, on court's asking this witness has deposed further that she realizes rents of two of the rooms of the suit land, but she could not tell the name of her tenants and also could not produce any receipts showing realization of rent from the tenants.

22. The DW 2 is the wife of the plaintiff. This witness has deposed to the effect that the defendant purchased the suit land with the money of her husband. During cross-examination this witness has stated further that she resides with the defendant and that her brother's son feed her.

23. The DW 3 is the brother's son of the defendant, This witness though in his examination-in-chief stated to the effect that the defendant purchased the suit land with her own money and that the defendant has two tenants in the suit land and there are tenancy agreement, but this witness did not say that he saw the defendant to pay the consideration money for the suit land and could not produce any tenancy agreement deed to show that the defendant let out any room of the suit land to any tenants. In course of cross-examination this witness has stated that he is the heir of the defendant. So, obviously, this DW 3 is a most interested witness in this suit.

24. However, from the above stated evidence adduced by both the parties it appears that in this suit it has been well proved that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and the plaintiff has also paid the consideration money for the suit land. All the title deeds and also all types of receipts showing payment of holding tax, rent, electricity bill, water bill, gas bill etc. came before court from the custody of the plaintiff. The suit land was purchased by two deeds of the same date, one is lease deed and another is kabala deed. The kabala deed came from the custody of the plaintiff and has been marked as Exhibit-13. The lease deed only came from the custody of the defendant, but the plaintiff has categorically stated both in his pleading and in deposition that the defendant, being asked by the plaintiff, took back that lease deed from the House Building Finance Corporation, but thereafter being, ill advised by others, she denied to give back that deed to the plaintiff. The plaintiff has proved also this case by examining witness. On the other hand the defendant could not adduce a single disinterested witness to support her case. The DW 2 though is the wife of the plaintiff, but from the evidence of this DW 2 herself it has been proved that this DW 2 has been residing with the defendant and is being fed by DW 3. This DW 3 also is a most interested witness who, being the heir of the defendant, will be most benefited if this suit is dismissed. It appears that the appellate court below the last court of fact, on consideration of all these evidence adduced by both the parties, found the plaintiffs case proved. The High Court Division, without making any discussion of any evidence adduced by the parties and without giving any reasoning for setting aside the well-reasoned judgment of the appellate court below set-aside the judgment of the appellate court below on the main reasoning that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant.

25. We have already pointed out above that in this suit it is an admitted fact that the plaintiff purchased the 'Kha' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant. So, in the circumstances, obviously, the trial court and the High Court Division committed a serious wrong in holding to the effect that there was no reason for the plaintiff to purchase the 'Ka' scheduled land in the 'benami' of the defendant.

26. However, we find that the appellate court below, on careful consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties and the facts and circumstances, rightly found the plaintiffs case proved and, therefore, rightly decreed the suit.

27. In this appeal another point needs to be addressed. The trial court found that this suit filed long 46 years after the execution and registration of the deed in question was barred by limitation. The appellate court below set-aside this finding and decision of the trail court making observations to the effect that the cause of action for this suit arose on the date on which the defendant denied to return the lease deed- the Exhibit-'Ka' to the plaintiff and also claimed ownership in the suit land. We find this finding and observation of the appellate court below correct. The plaintiff purchased the suit land in the 'benami' of the defendant in the year 1952 and since then he has been possessing the suit land and there did not arise any cause for declaration of the defendant as the 'benamder' of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land. Only when the defendant claimed ownership in the suit land the cause of action arose for the plaintiff to get the suit land in his name by declaring the defendant as his 'benamder'. The plaintiff filed this suit within the statutory period of limitation after the cause of action arose. So, this suit is not barred by limitation.

28. However, in view of the above discussion it is evident that this appeal deserves to be allowed.

Hence it is, ordered that this appeal be allowed on contest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division be set-aside and the judgment and decree of the appellate court below be restored.

End.
